name: Khaki (Web)
lede: Khaki (Web) is the paler, greyer version of [[khaki]] that the CSS and X11 color lists adopted for screens, and it turns up in one museum painting in six.

sections.title: The web's own khaki
sections.body:
Our color graph marks this swatch plainly as a web variant: the CSS and X11 keyword `khaki`, built from the same dust-colored word that named the fabric and the army uniform, but tuned for computer screens rather than cloth or paint [1]. The real dye khaki Lumsden's Guides wore at Peshawar in the 1840s, and the drab the First World War made famous, ran browner and more olive than this swatch; [[khaki|the fabric khaki]] in our library is a darker, more yellow-green shade than the pale, dusty tan the web keyword gives [1][2]. Nearby web and library names are [[putty]], at 2.6 units, and [[tan]] and [[long-beach|Long Beach]], both 4.0 to 4.3 units away [1].

Wikipedia is the only source in our library for the exact hex value, #C3B091, which our graph computes as a grayish yellow by ISCC-NBS block [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Our archive finds this tan in 3,868 of 23,781 paintings, about 16.3 percent, as photographed, with the stricter within-painting lens finding it in 2,659 [3]. It is more common than 97 percent of our named colors [3]. Inside a painting it most often plays a light tone, in 39 percent of its matches, rather than a shadow or an accent [3]. Willem van de Velde the Elder shows the heaviest use, in 7 of 14 of his works on file, nearly four times the rate expected from the museums that hold them [3]. The earliest matches run back to the 700s; that floor marks the limit of a thin early archive, not proof the color existed that early, since the match is a look-alike hue in an old varnished photograph, not a dye identification [3].
